title: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse environment

subtopics.heading: Boot methods
subtopics.notes:
How the installer reaches the machine:

- USB / flash drive: most common; motherboard must support USB boot
- Network (PXE - Preboot eXecution Environment): BIOS pulls the installer from a PXE server on the LAN. Useful when you cannot visit every machine
- Solid-state / flash drive: same as USB but using NVMe / SSD form factor
- Internet-based: minimal local boot, downloads the rest. macOS Recovery and Windows Update both work this way. Some Linux distros do this too
- External / hot-swappable drive: ISO mounted from an external drive that appears as a physical disk
- Internal hard drive (partition): installer files copied to a local partition, then boot from there
- Multi-boot: more than one OS installed on the same physical device, chosen at startup

ISO image: an exact copy of an optical disc as a single file. Common for virtualization and external mountable drives.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Match the scenario to the right boot method. PXE = no physical visits / remote install. Internet-based = recovery / minimal media.
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking 'recovery partition' as a boot method when the scenario describes a network-only install. Recovery partition is local.

subtopics.heading: Types of installations
subtopics.notes:
- Clean install: wipe the partition, install fresh. Nothing previous remains
- In-place upgrade: keeps apps, data, and user settings. Newer OS layered over the old one
- Image deployment: build one reference image (OS + apps + config), then push it to many machines
- Remote network installation: install files served from a network share, no local media required
- Zero-touch deployment: fully automated install + configuration. User opens a laptop, turns it on, walks away
- Recovery partition: hidden local partition with installer files. Useful for repair / re-install in the field
- Repair installation: Windows-specific. Overwrites OS files but keeps user data and configuration
- Third-party drivers: load during install (usually a prompt) when stock drivers don't recognize the storage controller or NIC
subtopics.whyOnExam: Know the difference between clean install (wipes everything) and in-place upgrade (keeps everything). Zero-touch deployment is the answer for 'ship a new laptop to a remote user'.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing 'repair installation' (keeps user data) with 'clean install' (does not). Repair fixes a broken OS without forcing a backup-restore cycle.

subtopics.heading: Partitioning: GPT vs MBR
subtopics.notes:
GPT (GUID Partition Table)
- Modern, requires UEFI BIOS
- Up to 128 partitions per drive, all equal type
- Theoretical drive size over 9 billion TB; Windows caps GPT volumes at 256 TB
- Simpler model (no primary/extended distinction)

MBR (Master Boot Record)
- Legacy, used before UEFI
- Maximum partition size 2 TB
- Maximum 4 primary partitions per drive
- Only one primary partition is active (bootable)
- For more than 4 partitions: use 1 extended partition holding multiple logical partitions. Logical partitions are NOT bootable

Volume vs partition (Microsoft term): a volume is just a formatted partition.

BIOS compatibility mode lets older BIOS boot GPT-style, but disables Secure Boot. Many newer OSes will not run without Secure Boot.
subtopics.whyOnExam: GPT requires UEFI. MBR caps at 2 TB and 4 primary partitions. Memorize the numbers.
subtopics.commonTrap: Saying 'extended partitions are bootable' on MBR. Only primary partitions boot; the extended one holds logical partitions which do not.

subtopics.heading: Drive format: quick vs full
subtopics.notes:
Quick format
- Builds a new file system table only
- Does NOT verify the physical disk
- Old data is technically recoverable with the right tool
- Default in Windows 10 and 11 installation

Full format
- Writes zeros across the entire disk
- Verifies disk sectors
- Old data is unrecoverable (more secure)
- Slow on large drives
- Triggered through the diskpart utility on Windows

Use quick when you trust the drive and need speed. Use full when the disk leaves your custody or contained sensitive data.
subtopics.whyOnExam: If a question mentions 'secure' or 'sanitization', pick full format. If it mentions 'fastest' or default install, pick quick.
subtopics.commonTrap: Assuming quick format actually erases the data. It only removes the table. Forensic tools can still recover much of the previous content.

subtopics.heading: Upgrade considerations
subtopics.notes:
Before upgrading:
- Back up user files and preferences (even on an in-place upgrade)
- Check application and driver compatibility against the new OS
- Check hardware requirements: CPU, RAM, free disk space
- Use vendor compatibility tools where available (Windows 11: PC Health Check)
- Have license keys ready

Feature updates vs quality updates:
- Quality updates: monthly security and bug fixes
- Feature updates: new capabilities, every 6-12 months
- Most Windows versions are supported 18-36 months under Microsoft's Modern Lifecycle Policy
subtopics.whyOnExam: PC Health Check is the specific tool name Microsoft uses for Windows 11 compatibility checks. Know it.
subtopics.commonTrap: Skipping the backup step before an in-place upgrade. Even though in-place 'keeps everything', upgrades can fail, and the backup is your only recovery path.

subtopics.heading: Windows 11 hardware requirements
subtopics.notes:
Windows 11 cannot install without:
- TPM 2.0 or later (Trusted Platform Module, cryptographic hardware on the motherboard). Check with tpm.msc
- UEFI BIOS (not legacy BIOS)
- Secure Boot enabled. Check the System Information utility under System Summary - look for 'Secure Boot State'
- A supported 64-bit CPU (Windows 11 dropped 32-bit support entirely)
- Sufficient RAM and storage

TPM 2.0 is also required for BitLocker and Windows Hello.

If the motherboard does not support UEFI or TPM 2.0, the machine usually cannot be upgraded - it must be replaced.
subtopics.whyOnExam: TPM 2.0 + UEFI + Secure Boot are the three big Windows 11 gates. Expect a scenario where one is missing and you must identify which.
subtopics.commonTrap: Picking 'more RAM' as the fix when the actual block is TPM or Secure Boot. Hardware-platform requirements come first.
